analogy.p: Imagine catching a water balloon. If you hold your hands still, the balloon stops almost instantly and bursts because the force is huge. If you move your hands back with the balloon, you stop it over a longer time and it survives. The balloon's change in momentum is the same either way, but the longer time makes the rate of change of momentum (the force) smaller. This is the same as an air bag. The analogy breaks down because a balloon bursts at a fixed force, whereas injury to a person depends on many factors such as which body part and how the force is spread.

bullets: **Force = rate of change of momentum.**
In symbols: **F = Δp ÷ Δt**, or **F = (m v − m u) ÷ t**.
**F** = resultant force in newtons (N); **m** = mass in kg; **v** = final velocity and **u** = initial velocity in m/s; **t** = time in seconds (s).
Momentum changes in the **same direction as the resultant force**.
A bigger force produces a bigger change in momentum in a given time, or the same change in a shorter time.
This is the Higher tier (HT) form of Newton's second law, and **F = m a** is the special case when mass is constant.
core.h: Force as the rate of change of momentum
core.p: At Higher tier you must know that **force equals the rate of change of momentum**. This is the most general form of **Newton's second law**. It says that a resultant force acting on an object changes its momentum, and the bigger the force, the faster the momentum changes. The word 'rate' means 'per unit time', so the force is the change in momentum divided by the time taken for the change. This is more powerful than F = m a because it still works when we only know about momentum before and after, for example in a crash or when a ball is hit.

bullets: **F = m Δv ÷ Δt** (force in N, mass in kg, Δv in m/s, Δt in s).
Rearranged: **Δt = m Δv ÷ F**, and **Δv = F Δt ÷ m**.
Change in momentum = **mass × change in velocity** = m(v − u).
**1 N = 1 kg m/s²** and equivalently 1 N = 1 kg m/s per second.
Always convert time from milliseconds: 4 ms = 0.004 s.
Check direction: a **negative** force means it acts opposite to the direction you called positive (for example a braking force).
If the answer is a force in a crash it is often very large (thousands of newtons) - that is normal.
core.h: The equation F = m Δv ÷ Δt and its units
core.p: The spec equation is **force = change in momentum ÷ time taken**, written **F = (m Δv) ÷ Δt**. Here **m Δv** is the change in momentum, found as the final momentum minus the initial momentum. The unit of momentum is kg m/s and time is in seconds, so the unit of force works out as (kg m/s) ÷ s = **kg m/s²**, which is exactly one **newton (N)**. Rearranged, **Δt = m Δv ÷ F** gives the time needed, and **m Δv = F Δt** gives the change in momentum produced by a force acting for a given time.

bullets: Start: **a = (v − u) ÷ t**.
Then F = m a becomes **F = m (v − u) ÷ t** = (m v − m u) ÷ t.
(m v − m u) is the **change in momentum**, so **F = Δp ÷ Δt**.
Both equations give the **same numerical answer** for constant mass - use whichever fits the data given.
'Show that' questions: write the steps above in order, naming each substitution.
This proves a larger force or a longer time means a larger change in momentum (and therefore in velocity).
core.p: You can show that the momentum form contains F = m a. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: **a = Δv ÷ Δt**. Substituting this into F = m a gives **F = m × (Δv ÷ Δt) = m Δv ÷ Δt**, which is the change in momentum divided by time. So the two equations say the same thing when the mass is constant. The momentum form is more general because it can also be used when mass changes (for example a rocket burning fuel) and it focuses on what is conserved, which makes it ideal for impact problems.

bullets: Momentum change is fixed by the **mass and velocity** of the person: the same Δp in every case.
Increasing the **time of the collision** reduces the **rate of change of momentum**.
Reduced rate of change of momentum means a **smaller force** on the person.
A smaller force means a **smaller deceleration** (a = F ÷ m), so less injury.
Example: stopping in 0.6 s instead of 0.15 s makes the force **four times smaller** (0.6 ÷ 0.15 = 4).
Model sentence: 'The safety feature increases the time of the collision, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on the passenger is smaller.'
core.h: Why a longer time means a smaller force
core.p: The key idea behind all safety features is that for a **given change in momentum**, the force depends on the **time** over which the change happens. If the time is **increased**, the **rate of change of momentum decreases**, so the **force decreases**. Think of F = Δp ÷ Δt: for the same Δp, doubling Δt halves F. A person in a crash has to lose all their momentum whatever happens; safety features cannot change this total, but they can spread it over a longer time so the force on the body is smaller and less likely to cause injury.

bullets: **Air bags**: inflate and the head/chest sinks into them, so the passenger stops over a **longer time**; they also spread the force over a **larger area**, reducing pressure.
**Seat belts**: stretch slightly (and are designed to) so the wearer slows down more gradually and is held in place; they stop the person hitting the windscreen.
**Crumple zones**: the front and rear of the car **crumple** on impact, increasing the stopping time of the car and the passengers.
**Cycle helmets**: the foam layer compresses so the head stops over a longer time.
**Crash mats/gym mats**: the soft mat compresses so the athlete's stopping time increases.
**Bending your knees** when landing, or **moving your hands back** when catching a ball: both lengthen the stopping time.
**Cushioned playground surfaces** and **padding on equipment** work the same way.
**Collapsible steering columns** reduce force on the driver's chest.
core.h: Safety features that use this idea
core.p: Many everyday devices are designed to **increase the collision time**. They do this by being deformable, moving back, or stretching so that the person or object takes longer to stop. In all cases the explanation has the same three steps: the time to stop is longer, therefore the rate of change of momentum (the force) is smaller, therefore there is less injury. You are expected to **explain** how at least air bags, seat belts, crumple zones, cycle helmets and crash mats work, and to apply the idea to new examples like catching a ball or bending your knees when you land.

bullets: Kinetic energy to be transferred: **½ m v²**, the same whatever the safety feature.
Work done **W = F × s**, so **F = W ÷ s**: a larger stopping distance means a smaller force.
Crumple zones increase both the **distance** and the **time** of the crash.
When a car stops in a short distance (a rigid wall) the force is much greater.
Do not say that safety features 'reduce the momentum' or 'reduce the energy' - those are fixed; they reduce the **force**.
Do not say the force is 'absorbed' without saying why: it is because time/distance is increased.
core.h: Time, distance and energy: a second explanation
core.p: The same safety features can also be explained using **work done and energy**. In stopping, the kinetic energy of the person has to be transferred. Work done = force × distance, so if the **stopping distance is increased**, the **force needed is smaller** for the same energy transfer. Crumple zones and air bags increase the distance as well as the time. Both explanations are valid at GCSE: mark schemes accept 'increases the time of impact so the force is smaller' (momentum approach), and some accept 'increases the distance over which the car stops so less force is needed' (energy approach). Use the one the question asks for, or give both in a 4 or 6 mark answer.

bullets: **1.** Write down m, u, v, t; convert to kg, m/s and seconds.
**2.** Choose a positive direction and give signs to velocities.
**3.** Change in momentum = m v − m u.
**4.** F = change in momentum ÷ t.
**5.** Quote the answer in newtons and state the direction of the force (the direction of the momentum **change**).
**6.** Sense-check: collision forces are large because the times are tiny.
Stopping from speed in a given time: v = 0, so Δp = −m u (momentum lost); the force is the **braking** or **impact** force.
For a rebound: Δv = v − (−u) = v + u (add the speeds).
core.p: Calculations on force and momentum change follow a fixed pattern. Identify the mass, the initial and final velocities (with signs), and the time of the collision. Work out the **change in momentum**, then divide by the time to get the **force**. If the object bounces back, the final velocity has the **opposite sign**, so the change in velocity is larger than the speed itself: for example a ball arriving at 25 m/s and leaving at 15 m/s the other way has a change in velocity of 40 m/s, not 10 m/s. This is the most common source of lost marks in this topic.

bullets: Same Δp: **tall narrow** force-time peak (short time) = big force; **low wide** curve (long time) = small force.
**Area under force-time graph = change in momentum** (extension idea).
Gradient of a velocity-time graph = **acceleration**, so force = mass × gradient.
In data tables, **calculate Δp for each row first** and then divide by time to compare forces.
When comparing two crashes, say: 'the force is smaller because the time is longer (for the same change in momentum)'.
Quote values with units in your answer and compare using numbers (for example 'four times smaller').
core.p: Exam questions often give a table of times and forces, or ask you to compare collisions. On a **force-time graph**, the **area under the graph equals the change in momentum** (this is the idea of impulse, F × t, an extension not required by name). A short, sharp peak of high force and a long, low force can have the **same area**, meaning the same change in momentum, which is exactly the idea behind safety features. On a **velocity-time graph** for a vehicle, the gradient is acceleration, and multiplying by mass gives the force.

bullets: Equal and opposite **forces** act for the **same time**, so the momentum changes are **equal and opposite**.
The force is the same size on both objects, but acceleration a = F ÷ m is **larger for the lighter object**.
The lighter vehicle's occupants suffer a **greater change in velocity** in a collision with a heavier vehicle.
This is the same idea as conservation of momentum, seen from the force side.
When a rocket pushes gas backwards with a force, the gas pushes the rocket forwards with an equal force.
Use the third law explicitly in 'explain' answers: 'the forces are equal and opposite'.
core.h: Link to Newton's third law and conservation of momentum
core.p: Newton's third law says that when a car hits a wall, the wall exerts a force on the car equal in size and opposite in direction to the force of the car on the wall. Because the forces act for the same time, the change in momentum of each is equal and opposite. This ties force-momentum to conservation of momentum: if object A gains momentum Δp, object B must lose Δp in the same time, so the two forces F = Δp ÷ Δt are equal and opposite. This is why a small insect and a lorry experience the same-size force in a collision, but very different accelerations because of their different masses.

bullets: For braking: **F = m Δv ÷ Δt** with final velocity zero.
Greater speed means greater momentum, so for the same force, **more time and distance** are needed.
A bigger mass means greater momentum, so more force or more time is needed.
Reduced friction (wet/icy roads, worn tyres) reduces the braking force that can be applied.
Large decelerations cause **very large forces** on passengers, which is why safety features matter.
Thinking distance is unaffected by braking force; only braking distance is.
core.h: Link to stopping distances and braking
core.p: The braking part of the stopping distance involves a force changing the momentum of the car. A larger braking force makes the momentum fall faster, so the car stops in a shorter time and distance. If the car's speed is higher, its momentum is higher and more momentum must be removed, so for a given braking force the stopping time (and distance) is longer. Anything that reduces the braking force (worn brakes, wet or icy roads, worn tyres) makes the time to stop longer. If the braking force is too large the deceleration may be dangerous (it can cause skidding or injury), which is why braking forces are limited.

bullets: Thrust of a rocket = **rate of change of momentum of the exhaust gas**.
**Follow-through** lengthens the contact time, giving the ball a bigger change in momentum (F Δt = Δp).
**Catching**: pulling the hands back increases the time and so decreases the force on the hands.
**Karate/boxing**: a short contact time with a high speed gives a very large force.
Hosepipe or water-jet forces: the water's momentum changes quickly when it hits a wall, producing a force.
In all cases the key relationship is **F = Δp ÷ Δt**.
core.h: Higher tier extension: rockets, sport and variable mass
core.p: The momentum form of Newton's second law can be applied to cases where mass changes. In a rocket, hot gas leaves the engine at high speed, each second a certain mass of gas gains backwards momentum, and the rocket gains an equal forward momentum per second, which is the thrust. In sport, a longer follow-through gives the ball a longer contact time with the bat, so for a given force the change in momentum is larger and the ball leaves faster. Batters 'give' with the ball when catching to extend the stopping time and reduce the sting.

exam: **Recall** (1 mark): 'force = rate of change of momentum' or the equation F = m Δv ÷ Δt with symbols defined.
**Calculate** (3 marks): 1 mark for Δp (or Δv) correct, 1 for dividing by time, 1 for answer with unit (N).
**Explain how a safety feature reduces injury** (3 marks): 'increases the time of the collision' (1), 'so the rate of change of momentum decreases' (1), 'so the force on the person is smaller' (1).
**Model phrase**: 'The change in momentum is the same but it happens over a longer time, so the force is smaller.' Use this in every explanation.
**4 and 6 mark** answers: link time, rate of change of momentum, force, then deceleration and injury; refer to the specific feature (stretch, crumple, compress).
**Command words**: 'Explain' needs a reason with 'because/so'; 'Calculate' needs working; 'Show that' needs all steps and a final value matching the one given.
**Show that F = m Δv ÷ Δt** follows from F = m a: substitute a = Δv ÷ Δt and state the result.
**Rebound questions**: add speeds if direction reverses; marks are lost for subtracting.
**Graph tips**: for equal area force-time graphs, say 'same change in momentum'; taller peak = bigger force.
**Comparisons**: use numbers - 'the force is four times smaller because the time is four times longer'.
Check units: kg m/s ÷ s = N, and answer to the same number of significant figures as the data.

mistakes.r: The momentum change is the same; the air bag increases the time of the collision, so the rate of change of momentum, and so the force, is smaller.
mistakes.w: 'The air bag reduces the momentum' or 'absorbs the force'.

mistakes.r: If direction reverses, add the speeds: Δv = 15 − (−25) = 40 m/s.
mistakes.w: Calculating a rebound change in velocity as the difference of speeds (25 − 15).
Leaving time in milliseconds when using F = Δp ÷ Δt.

mistakes.r: Force is in newtons (N); momentum is in kg m/s.
mistakes.w: Writing the unit of force as kg m/s.

mistakes.r: Say: longer time → smaller rate of change of momentum → smaller force on the passenger.
mistakes.w: Saying a longer time reduces the 'impact' or 'speed' without stating force.

mistakes.r: They increase the time taken to stop, which reduces the force (the crumple zone does not make the car stop sooner).
mistakes.w: Saying safety features stop the car quicker.

mistakes.r: Check: Δp = m(v − u), then F = Δp ÷ t; no squares are involved.
mistakes.w: Using the mass of the wrong object, or forgetting to square or divide properly.

mistakes.r: By Newton's third law, the forces are equal and opposite; the lighter vehicle has the larger acceleration.
mistakes.w: Saying the forces in a collision are bigger on the lighter vehicle.

mistakes.r: If the question gives velocities and a time, use F = m Δv ÷ Δt (or show a = Δv ÷ t first).
mistakes.w: Giving F = m a only when asked to use momentum.

summary: At Higher tier the spec asks you to recall and apply F = m Δv ÷ Δt (force is the rate of change of momentum) and to explain how safety features such as air bags, seat belts and crumple zones reduce injury by increasing the time over which momentum changes. It matters because it links Newton's second law to real-life collisions and is regularly tested in 4 to 6 mark explain questions.

terms.d: Mass × velocity (p = m v); a vector quantity measured in kg m/s.
Final momentum minus initial momentum, Δp = m v − m u.
The change in momentum divided by the time taken for the change (Δp ÷ Δt); equal to the resultant force.
The single force that has the same effect as all of the forces acting on an object.
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass; in momentum form, force equals rate of change of momentum.
Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
The unit of force; 1 N = 1 kg m/s².
The time during which two objects are in contact and exert forces on each other.
A negative acceleration; the rate at which an object slows down.
A safety device that inflates in a collision, increasing the time over which the occupant stops and spreading the force over a larger area.
A restraint that stretches slightly, increasing stopping time and holding the occupant in place.
A part of a vehicle designed to deform on impact, increasing the time (and distance) of the collision.
A system with no external forces, in which the total momentum is conserved.
Energy of a moving object, ½ m v².
Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance; W = F s.

worked.ans: The air bag increases the time over which the driver's momentum changes (1). This decreases the rate of change of momentum (1), so the force acting on the driver is smaller, reducing injury (1).
worked.q: Explain how an air bag reduces the risk of serious injury to a driver in a head-on collision. (3 marks)
steps: Say what changes: the driver's momentum falls to zero over the collision.
Say what the air bag does: it compresses so it increases the time taken for the driver to stop.
Link to force: this reduces the rate of change of momentum, so the force on the driver is smaller.
